# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer a range of features to facilitate collaboration, communication, and productivity. The core use case for both tools is team messaging, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data Ownership: Element allows users to have full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Slack has better scalability features, while Element can be more challenging to scale for large teams.
* Integration: Slack has a wider range of integrations with third-party apps, while Element has a more limited selection.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Scalable for large teams
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data
* Customizable and extensible
* Secure and private
* Limited integrations with third-party apps

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and have a large budget for communication tools. It's ideal for teams with 50-500 users who need a wide range of integrations and good customer support. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that value data ownership and security. It's ideal for teams with 10-50 users who are technically savvy and want a customizable and extensible communication platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data in JSON format using the Slack API.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data.
4. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.
5. Train your team on how to use Element and its features.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability features are not as robust as Slack's. However, for teams that value data ownership and security, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching if you have a small to medium-sized team and are technically savvy.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (10-20 users) who value data ownership and security
* Teams who do not need a wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Technically savvy teams who can set up and maintain an Element server
* Teams who are looking for a free and self-hosted communication platform
* Teams who prioritize customization and extensibility

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any subscription fees. However, you will need to pay for server costs.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element is not as easy to use as Slack, as it requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain.
### Can I integrate Element with third-party apps?
Yes, Element has a limited range of integrations with third-party apps, but it is not as extensive as Slack's.
### Is Element secure and private?
Yes, Element is secure and private, as it allows users to have full control over their data and communications.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can migrate your Slack data to Element using the Element import tool and the Slack API.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for team collaboration. Both tools offer a range of features to facilitate communication, file sharing, and project management, making them ideal for businesses, organizations, and communities. The core use case for both tools is to provide a centralized platform for team communication, and the key reason someone would switch from Slack to Mattermost is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges a per-user fee.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows users to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up and requires less technical expertise, while Mattermost requires more technical knowledge to self-host.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to be highly scalable and can handle large teams and high traffic, while Slack also offers scalable plans but at a higher cost.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost offers native integration with GitHub, while Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Mattermost:**
* Free, self-hosted option
* High degree of customizability
* Strong focus on security and data ownership
* Scalable and performant
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations. It's also a good option for teams who don't require a high degree of control over their data and are willing to pay a per-user fee. Mattermost, on the other hand, is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of control over their data and security. It's also a good option for teams who are looking for a self-hosted solution and are comfortable with the technical requirements.

Mattermost is also a good choice for teams who are already using other self-hosted tools and want to integrate their communication platform with their existing infrastructure. For example, teams who are using GitLab or GitHub for version control may appreciate Mattermost's native integration with these tools. Additionally, teams who are concerned about data sovereignty and want to ensure that their data is stored on their own servers may prefer Mattermost's self-hosted option.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool like Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data into Mattermost.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with third-party apps.
5. Test your Mattermost setup to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many users, offering a high degree of customizability and control over data storage and security. However, it's worth noting that Mattermost's self-hosted option can be more complex to set up and require more technical expertise than Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's search functionality can be slower than Slack's, especially for large teams with a high volume of messages.

Mattermost's self-hosted option also requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain, which can be a barrier for some teams. However, for teams who are willing to invest the time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own Mattermost server, the benefits can be significant. For example, teams who are concerned about data sovereignty and want to ensure that their data is stored on their own servers may find that the extra complexity is worth it.

Overall, we recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a large team or organization that requires a high degree of control over your data and security, and are willing to invest the time and resources into setting up and maintaining your own server. However, if you're a small team who just needs a simple, easy-to-use communication platform, Slack may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) who require a high degree of control over their data and security
* Teams who are already using self-hosted tools and want to integrate their communication platform with their existing infrastructure
* Organizations who are concerned about data sovereignty and want to ensure that their data is stored on their own servers
* Teams who don't need a wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Teams who are looking for a free or low-cost communication platform and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option that allows you to host your own server and have full control over your data.

### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost can be more complex to set up and use than Slack, especially for teams who are not familiar with self-hosted tools.

### Can I integrate Mattermost with third-party apps?
Yes, Mattermost offers a wide range of integrations with third-party apps, including GitHub, GitLab, and many others.

### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool and then import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.

### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
It depends on the team's specific needs and requirements. If the team is looking for a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations, Slack may be a better choice. However, if the team is looking for a free or low-cost solution and is willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own server, Mattermost may be a good option.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for communities and teams, offering features such as chat, voice and video conferencing, and file sharing. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being secure and customizable team communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce dependence on third-party services.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to self-host and retain full ownership of their data, whereas Discord stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Element is designed to be highly scalable, with support for large communities and teams, whereas Discord's free plan has limitations on the number of users and features.
* Integration: Element has native integration with the Matrix protocol, allowing for seamless communication with other Matrix-compatible platforms, whereas Discord has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Discord
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Robust feature set, including screen sharing and video conferencing
* Mobile apps available
* Limited control over data and customization options
### Element
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Open-source and highly customizable
* Scalable and suitable for large communities
* Native integration with Matrix protocol
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or communities that prioritize ease of use and a robust feature set, and are willing to compromise on data control and customization. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for larger organizations or communities that require high scalability, customization, and control over their data, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord server data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure the necessary settings and integrations.
3. Import your Discord data into Element using the Matrix API or a compatible import tool.
4. Test and verify that all features and data are working as expected.
5. Update your community or team on the migration and provide guidance on using the new platform.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires significant technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's self-hosting option requires a strong understanding of server management and maintenance. However, for teams and communities that value data control and customization, Element is a viable alternative to Discord, and we recommend switching for those who are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution.

## Who Should Switch

* Medium-sized communities (10-50 users) that need scalable and secure communication
* Large organizations (50+ users) that prioritize data ownership and control
* Communities that do not require advanced features like screen sharing or video conferencing
* Teams that are already familiar with the Matrix protocol or have experience with self-hosting

## FAQ

Yes, Element is free and open-source, with optional self-hosting.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
No, Element uses the Matrix protocol, which is not compatible with Discord.
### Can I migrate my Discord data to Element?

# Notion vs AppFlowy

## Overview

Notion is a popular all-in-one workspace combining notes, wikis, databases, and project management. AppFlowy is an open-source alternative with a local-first architecture that keeps your data on your device or own server.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; AppFlowy is completely free
- **Data location**: AppFlowy stores data locally by default; Notion stores on their servers
- **Offline support**: AppFlowy works fully offline; Notion requires internet for most features
- **Privacy**: AppFlowy does not collect usage data; Notion privacy policy allows data analysis
- **Feature parity**: Notion has more polished features and AI tools; AppFlowy is rapidly catching up

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### AppFlowy

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy](https://github.com/AppFlowy-IO/AppFlowy) * ~59k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion suits teams wanting a polished workspace with AI writing tools and seamless collaboration without managing infrastructure.

**Choose AppFlowy if:** AppFlowy is ideal for privacy-conscious individuals, users in regions with data sovereignty requirements, or anyone needing offline-first functionality.

## Migration Path

Export your Notion workspace as Markdown plus CSV files, then import the Markdown files into AppFlowy. Database structures will need to be recreated manually.

## Our Take

AppFlowy is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your AppFlowy instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted AppFlowy will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is AppFlowy free to use?
Yes. AppFlowy is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to AppFlowy?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the AppFlowy import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does AppFlowy get regular updates?
Yes. AppFlowy has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use AppFlowy without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if AppFlowy development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [AppFlowy](https://appflowy.io) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms used for software development, collaborating with teams, and managing projects. This comparison benefits developers, project managers, and organizations looking to choose between the two or switch from one to the other, primarily due to differences in cost, data ownership, and specific feature sets. The core use case for both platforms is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free accounts with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows for self-hosting, giving users full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitLab can be more complex to set up, especially for self-hosting, compared to GitHub's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: GitLab is designed to handle large, complex projects and teams, while GitHub is also scalable but may require more configuration.
* Specific feature difference: GitLab offers built-in Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tools, whereas GitHub relies on third-party integrations for CI/CD.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Easy to set up and use
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers free accounts with limited features
* Limited control over data for free accounts
### GitLab
* Offers self-hosting for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD tools
* Highly scalable and customizable
* Free self-hosted option with many features
* Can be complex to set up, especially for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or projects that require a simple, easy-to-use version control platform with a large community and ecosystem. It's ideal for teams that don't need full control over their data and are willing to pay for additional features. GitLab, on the other hand, is designed for larger, more complex projects and teams that require high scalability, customization, and control over their data. It's ideal for teams that need built-in CI/CD tools and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring the platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which creates a ZIP file containing your repository's data.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the repository settings.
3. Use the GitLab import tool to import your GitHub repository data from the ZIP file.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as CI/CD pipelines and permissions.
5. Verify that your repository has been successfully migrated by checking the repository contents and testing any CI/CD pipelines.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and high scalability. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's self-hosted option can be complex to set up and require significant resources. For teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setup and configuration, GitLab is a clear choice. However, for small teams or projects that don't need advanced features, GitHub may still be the better option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that need full control over their data and are willing to self-host
* Large teams that require high scalability and customization
* Teams that need built-in CI/CD tools and are currently using third-party integrations on GitHub
* Teams that are currently paying for GitHub features and can save costs by switching to GitLab's free self-hosted option
* Teams that don't need GitHub's large community and ecosystem and prefer a more customizable platform

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with many features, as well as a free SaaS option with limited features.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab suitable for small teams?
Yes, GitLab can be suitable for small teams, especially those that need full control over their data and are willing to self-host.
### Does GitLab offer CI/CD tools?
Yes, GitLab offers built-in CI/CD tools.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, you can migrate your GitHub repository to GitLab using the GitHub export tool and the GitLab import tool.

title: GitHub vs Gitea
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by product teams, designers, and developers to create user interfaces and user experiences. This comparison is beneficial for teams looking to transition from a proprietary design tool to an open-source alternative.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a range of plans, including a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: With Penpot, users have full control over their design data, whereas Figma stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, while Penpot is still developing its scalability features.
* Integration difference: Figma has a more extensive library of third-party plugins and integrations, whereas Penpot has a growing but limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

* Pros:
  + User-friendly interface
  + Robust feature set
  + Large community and support resources
  + Extensive library of plugins and integrations
  + Scalable for large teams and projects
* Cons:
  + Expensive, especially for large teams

* Cons:

  + Limited scalability features

Figma is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a robust and scalable design tool with a wide range of features and integrations. On the other hand, Penpot is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, startups, and individuals who value control over their design data and are looking for a free and open-source alternative. It's also a good choice for teams with technical expertise and resources to set up and maintain a self-hosted design tool.

## Migration Path

## Our Take
Penpot is still a relatively new and developing design tool, and while it shows great promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's scalability features are still in development, which may impact large teams and complex projects. ## Who Should Switch

* Startups and individuals who prioritize control over design data

### Can I use Penpot for free?

### Is Penpot self-hostable?
Yes, Penpot offers self-hosting options, allowing users to have full control over their design data and infrastructure.
### Does Penpot support real-time collaboration?
